headline: Scam compensation: the law says courts 'shall' order it, if prosecutors ask
context: Money traced in time can be frozen and handed back to scam victims. When it is gone, CPC s.426(1A) lets a court order the convicted offender to pay compensation instead.

cards.big: Since 2012, Malaysian courts must order convicts to compensate victims when prosecutors ask. We found no published count of how often they ask in scam cases.
cards.sub: CPC s.426(1A). The court sets the sum and weighs the convict's ability to pay. Before 2012, such orders were at the court's discretion.
trace: CPC (Act 593), AGC updated text as at 4 Jul 2023, s.426(1A): court 'shall, upon the application of the Public Prosecution, make an order against the convicted accused for the payment by him ... of a sum to be fixed by the Court as compensation to a person who is the victim of the offence'; s.426(1C)(f) 'the ability of the convicted accused to pay' (Stage 3 VERIFIED; Stage 2 VERIFIED).

In force 1 Jun 2012 (AGC amendment table, Acts A1378/A1422; Stage 3 VERIFIED on date). Pre-2012 discretion: CPC 2006 reprint s.426(1)(b) 'may, in its discretion' (Stage 3 omitted fact; ICJ copy of the official reprint p.177).

'We found no published count': bounded search finding per Stage 3 correction (searches of BNM, Home Ministry, AGC and court publications and EN/MS news to 8 Nov 2026; brief REBUILD RESEARCH Q3 and SECOND INDEPENDENT VERIFICATION).

cards.big: Attorney General Dusuki Mokhtar ordered prosecutors to seek compensation orders for crime victims 'in the appropriate cases', FMT reported on 15 April 2026.
cards.sub: By FMT's account, he acknowledged such requests were not a conventional practice. The directive is general, not scam-specific.
trace: FMT, 'DPPs ordered to seek compensation for crime victims', 15 Apr 2026 (opened by editor 2026-11-07): AG 'ordered all deputy public prosecutors to apply for the courts to order compensation for the victims of crimes, including those killed by drivers driving under the influence'; 'in the appropriate cases'; reported speech that seeking compensation was not a conventional practice. Stage 3: attribution matches; official directive text not opened; card keeps 'FMT reported'.
Dropped 'not possible in all cases': Stage 3 found the Malay account (Berita Harian) describes incomplete implementation, not impossibility; unresolved without the original words.

cards.big: The scam response centre returned RM6.65m to victims in 2025, the Home Ministry told Parliament. Bank Negara put 2025's reported scam losses at RM2.8b.
cards.sub: Courts hand those returns back under CPC s.413. On 27 October the home minister told Parliament the government was not satisfied.
trace: Home Ministry written answer, 4 Feb 2026, Q82 (parlimen.gov.my JDR04022026): NSRC returns RM508,479.39 (2024) and RM6.65m (2025) (Stage 3 VERIFIED; Stage 6 could not reopen the PDF, connection reset).

BNM Annual Report 2025, Box 4 'Fraud Resolution' (opened by Stage 6): 'In Malaysia, the reported impact amounted to RM2.8 billion in 2025', note 2: PDRM data covering telecommunication, e-commerce, loan, investment and love scams plus malware and phishing.

Dewan Rakyat Hansard (draft), 27 Oct 2026 (opened by Stage 6): Saifuddin, RM14.3m returned 12 Oct 2022 to Sep 2026; 'apakah kita berpuas hati? Jawapannya, tidak sebab kerugian bagi penipuan atas talian ini ... besar.' The s.413 total matches the minister's returns total.

cards.big: Bank Negara reported 969 convictions of mule account holders in 2025. We found no count of compensation orders against any of them.
cards.sub: Courts weigh what a convict can pay, and orders reach only that offence's victim. We found no ruling on whether a scam victim qualifies. All 969 predate the directive.
trace: BNM Annual Report 2025, ch.1g p.97 (opened by Stage 6): 'In 2025, 969 convictions were secured against mule account holders.' No offence breakdown; card names no section.
s.426(1C)(f) ability to pay; s.426(1A) 'victim of the offence committed by the convicted accused' (Stage 3 VERIFIED). 'No ruling found' is the bounded wording Stage 3 accepted.
Convictions in 2025 predate the reported 15 Apr 2026 announcement (Stage 3 VERIFIED chronology).

cards.big: The 2012 law binds the judge once a prosecutor asks. It binds no one to ask.
trace: Paradox form. 'Binds the judge': s.426(1A) 'shall ... make an order' once the Public Prosecution applies. 'Binds no one to ask': the section imposes no duty to apply; the AG's directive is an internal instruction, not statute (CPC text, Stage 3 VERIFIED).

cards.big: If compensation hinges on prosecutorial discretion, the Attorney General's Chambers should publish the ledger: requests made, orders granted, and what victims are actually paid.
trace: Editorial view. 'Prosecutorial discretion' follows from the 'upon the application of the Public Prosecution' trigger. The ledger items answer Stage 3's point that requests alone cannot show whether the law works: orders and actual payments are needed too (s.426(4) preserves civil recovery beyond sums actually paid).

synthesis_notes: Over-integration calls. (1) Stage 5 asked the view to call s.426(1A) a 'paper tiger' that 'has not been operationalised'; Stage 3 asked every absence claim to be bounded to the sources searched. These pull opposite ways and the evidence decides each part. The AG's reported acknowledgement that seeking compensation was not a conventional practice is evidence of non-routine use, so it goes on the card face, attributed. 'Paper tiger' and 'not operationalised' would assert a usage rate nobody has published, which Stage 5 itself conceded when it dropped 'never used'. The synthesis states the structural cause instead (reframe: the statute binds the judge, not the prosecutor) and asks for the ledger that would settle it (view). (2) Stage 2 and Stage 5 both wanted the scale of losses; Stage 1's guardrail kept losses off the cards because they are a different pool. The synthesis sides with Stages 2 and 5 on showing scale and with Stage 1 on not dividing: same-year returns (RM6.65m) and BNM's reported losses (RM2.8b) appear side by side with no ratio, and the minister's own 'not satisfied' remark shows the government reads the gap the same way. (3) Stage 3's most serious finding was that NSRC returns already run through courts under s.413, which made the old reframe's NSRC-versus-courts contrast false. The rebuilt issue rests on the distinction that survives: s.413 hands back traced money; s.426(1A) is what remains when the money is gone, and only it depends on a prosecutor asking. Declined suggestions, with reasons. (a) Stage 5's description of convicted mules as 'young, low-income, or foreign workers' and of masterminds as 'typically outside Malaysian jurisdiction': no primary source in the file profiles the 969 convictions; the card states the legal limit (ability to pay) without asserting the profile. (b) Stage 2's fix to explain that mule offences criminalise handing over accounts: Act A1721's offence text was not opened in this pass, so no card characterises ss.424A-424C; the card uses BNM's own phrase 'mule account holders'. (c) Stage 2's suggested reference to CPC s.413 as the main restitution route is adopted via the Economic sub. (d) Stage 2's '20 individuals from 51 cases' reconciliation: Stage 3 found it is a case-stage count, not comparable with BNM's 969; kept off cards. (e) Stage 5's prediction (no count by May 2027) is labelled HYPOTHESIS by Stage 5 and is not published. Compression decisions. (i) The Jan-May 2026 49% and 2022-2025 29% ratios are dropped: Stage 3 could not verify the window and attribution date, and the same-year 2025 figure is primary. (ii) RM14.3m cumulative returns stay in the trace, not on the card face, to keep one return figure per card. (iii) The AG's 'not possible in all cases' is dropped rather than softened, because English and Malay accounts differ in substance. (iv) 'Victim of the offence committed by the convicted accused' is compressed to 'only that offence's victim', preserving the qualifier. (v) Agrobank's RM1.505m order is kept off cards (bank's own funds; Stage 3 UNVERIFIED on inclusion in NSRC totals).
